content.text: This confirms the daemon mitigates the "reload GGUF every time" concern well. No MaxOpenConns setting found anywhere — confirms concurrency concern. Let me quickly check recall.go's nomicSearch and indexer.go's transaction handling.
I have enough to write the report. No `sql.Tx`/transactions used anywhere in indexer.go — each insert is autocommitted individually, which is relevant to the interrupted-migration/rebuild question.

Good — `rebuild` runs `DROP TABLE` then repopulates non-transactionally, meaning a kill mid-rebuild leaves `index.db` in a half-dropped state — though that's recoverable since index.db is always rebuildable. Data DB attaches READ_ONLY, which is good (git operations touching data.db won't corrupt it via rekal's own writes at least during index). Now I have sufficient evidence for all 5 areas.

findings.failure_scenario: A post-commit hook firing `rekal checkpoint` while a user runs `rekal index` or a background sync touches the same .rekal/data.db or index.db concurrently from two OS processes. go-duckdb/DuckDB's single-process-writer file locking will make one process fail to open or block; there's no retry/backoff, so the loser gets a raw 'open database: ...' error instead of a friendly 'rekal: another rekal pr...[truncated for fixture]
findings.summary: No SetMaxOpenConns/SetMaxIdleConns on database/sql handles for a single-writer embedded DuckDB file; concurrent rekal invocations (git hook checkpoint + background index) can race on data.db/index.db.

findings.failure_scenario: Process killed (OOM, ctrl-C, disk full) between DropIndexTables succeeding and PopulateIndex finishing: index.db now has some empty/missing tables and stale ones, and there is no 'rebuild in progress' marker, so a subsequent `rekal recall` silently queries a half-populated index instead of failing loudly or auto-detecting the inconsistency.
findings.summary: DropIndexTables + PopulateIndex (rekal index) run as a sequence of autocommitted DDL/DML statements with no wrapping transaction, so a kill mid-rebuild (or disk full) leaves index.db with some tables dropped/empty and others stale.

findings.failure_scenario: Not a bug today (call sites consistently COALESCE), but any new code path that reads team_name/workflow_name without COALESCE against a migrated (teammate-committed, pre-metadata) data.db will get NULL where the DDL comment implies NOT NULL is enforced — a latent trap for future contributors, not a live defect.
findings.summary: addColumnIfMissing strips NOT NULL from migrated columns and never re-applies it, so old-vs-new data.db rows have inconsistent nullability guarantees that downstream code must COALESCE around everywhere (already done, but fragile/no single source of truth).

findings.failure_scenario: Teammate A runs rekal v0.3.0 which adds a new NOT NULL-ish column to sessions; commits data.db. Teammate B still on v0.2.9 runs `rekal index` or `rekal checkpoint` against that data.db — DuckDB will happily open it and INSERT statements that don't reference the new column succeed, but any new column enforcing invariants B's version doesn't know about is silently bypassed with no version check or...[truncated for fixture]
findings.summary: No forward-compatibility handling or guard: a NEWER data.db (extra columns from a future rekal version, committed to git by a teammate on a newer build) opened by an OLDER rekal will silently ignore new columns rather than erroring, and there is no schema/version marker anywhere to detect this.

findings.failure_scenario: Many parallel `rekal recall` calls (e.g., scripted/CI) each dial the daemon and block on the shared mutex; not a correctness bug, just an unbounded-goroutine-per-connection design that could pile up if a client hangs (goroutine leak per stalled connection since handleConn's readMsg has no read deadline).
findings.summary: Idle timer reset only happens on the select loop goroutine when a new conn arrives or in handleConn per-request, but Accept() runs unbounded concurrent goroutines per connection sharing one embedder behind a mutex — fine for correctness, but a burst of parallel rekal invocations serializes on the single mutex-guarded model with no queuing/backpressure limit.
